opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think consumer choice matters more than people assume, but it works in a less direct way than the classic "vote with your wallet" story.

Most people aren't choosing AI products in isolation. They're choosing them embedded inside things they already use, like their phone, their email, their search engine, their workplace software. So a lot of the "choice" is really made upstream by a handful of companies deciding what gets bundled and set as the default. If an assistant shows up pre-installed and one tap away, it gets attention whether or not it's the best or most trustworthy option. That's the first thing I'd want listeners to understand: defaults are a form of choice architecture, and they quietly steer where attention flows.

That said, consumer behavior still sends powerful signals, because these products are measured obsessively. Engagement, retention, time spent, how often you come back. Every interaction becomes a data point that tells a company, "do more of this." And here's the tension. The metrics that are easiest to capture, like time on app or daily active use, don't necessarily line up with whether the product actually made someone's life better. An AI companion that keeps you talking for three hours might look like a huge success on a dashboard, even if you walk away lonelier or more dependent. So when we engage with something compulsively, we're inadvertently voting for more compulsion.

Where I see real leverage is when people shift from passive engagement to more deliberate signals. Paying for products whose business model isn't built on harvesting attention. Choosing tools that are transparent about how they use your data. Leaving products that feel manipulative, and saying why, publicly. Organizations and schools have even more leverage than individuals, because when they adopt something, they're making the choice for thousands of people at once, and they can demand standards up front.

But I'd be careful not to put the whole burden on consumers. It's a bit like asking individuals to fix pollution by recycling harder. Individual choices matter and they add up, but they work best alongside things like sensible regulation, honest disclosure, and design norms that make the humane option the easy option. Ideally, choosing well shouldn't require heroic effort. The healthiest outcome is one where the products that win attention are the ones that genuinely earn it, by respecting people's time, their autonomy, and their wellbeing.

r001.rationale: The candidate says consumer behavior sends signals to companies and that defaults and engagement steer where attention flows, framing consumer choices as influencing which AI products receive attention.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think consumers have more power here than they realize, but it's a power that gets exercised mostly by accident. Every time you pick up one app instead of another, or spend an extra ten minutes with a chatbot because it flattered you, you're casting a vote. And the companies are watching those votes very closely. Engagement metrics drive product roadmaps, product roadmaps drive investment, and investment drives which models get built next.

The problem is that the vote isn't really informed. Most people aren't choosing between "the AI that's honest with me" and "the AI that tells me what I want to hear." They're choosing between the one that's installed on their phone by default and the one that isn't. They're choosing the one that feels good in the moment. So attention flows toward whatever is most compelling, not toward whatever is most trustworthy or most useful over the long run.

That said, I don't want to be fatalistic about it. We've seen consumer sentiment shift industries before. People stopped trusting certain social platforms, and that mattered. There's a growing group of users who ask real questions now: Where does my data go? Is this thing designed to keep me hooked? Does it actually make my life better? When those questions start showing up in reviews, in churn numbers, in what people recommend to their friends, companies notice.

So my honest answer is that consumer choice is shaping what gets built, but right now it's shaping it in the direction of the most seductive products rather than the most humane ones. The work is to close that gap, to help people understand what they're actually choosing, so that the vote they're already casting lines up with what they'd want if they stepped back and thought about it.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing one AI product over another as casting a vote and says consumer attention flows toward products people find compelling.

astra-6.text: Consumers shape what gets attention through what they use, pay for, and share. If we consistently choose products that save us time and help us do something meaningful, that sends a different signal than rewarding products that simply keep us engaged. But I wouldn’t put all the responsibility on consumers. The choices we see are already shaped by companies—by what they promote, how they design the experience, and what they make easy to access. Consumer choice matters, but so does whether the industry gives people meaningful choices in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says consumers direct attention through the products they use, pay for, and share.

sol-6.1.text: I think consumers have a real role in deciding which AI products get attention. Every time we choose a product, pay for it, or recommend it to someone else, we’re sending a signal about what we value. The challenge is that what grabs our attention immediately isn’t always what serves us best over time. So I’d encourage people to ask: Is this actually helping me do something meaningful? Do I trust it? Does it respect my time? Those choices can push companies toward building more useful products, though consumers shouldn’t have to carry that responsibility alone.

r001.rationale: The response says choosing, paying for, or recommending an AI product sends a signal that helps decide which products get attention.
